A⋅x=cx+dax+b​,

with the usual conventions when the denominator vanishes or x=∞. Matrix multiplication agrees with composition, so this is a group action. If A fixes every projective point, then it fixes 0 and ∞, forcing b=c=0, and fixing 1 then gives a=d. Thus the kernel consists exactly of the nonzero scalar matrices Z. The induced group homomorphism
ϕ:GL2​(F)/Z⟶Sq+1​

ds2=y2dx2+dy2​

A function f:D→R on a convex set D is convex when
f((1−t)x+ty)≤(1−t)f(x)+tf(y)
(19)
for all x,y∈D and 0≤t≤1.
If f is once differentiable, this is equivalent to monotonicity of its gradient:
(∇f(x)−∇f(y))⋅(x−y)≥0​.
(20)
Equivalently, every tangent hyperplane supports the graph:
f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)⋅(y−x).
(21)
If f is twice differentiable, convexity is equivalent to the hessian matrix being positive semidefinite throughout D.
For
f(x,y)=x3+y3+Axy,
(22)
the Hessian is
H=(6xA​A6y​).
(23)
A real symmetric two-by-two matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when its two diagonal entries and its determinant are nonnegative. Thus
x≥0,y≥0,36xy−A2≥0.
(24)
The largest convexity domain is therefore
DA​={(x,y):x≥0, y≥0, 36xy≥A2}​.
(25)
For A=0, its boundary is the hyperbola y=A2/(36x) in the first quadrant and the domain lies above it. For A=0, it is the closed first quadrant. This is the convexity domain of x cubed plus y cubed plus Axy.

W=χ1​χ2′​−χ1′​χ2​

A linear operator α on a real inner-product space is self-adjoint when
⟨αv,w⟩=⟨v,αw⟩
(43)
for all v,w.
To prove the finite-dimensional spectral theorem, first note that the continuous quadratic function ⟨αv,v⟩ has a maximum on the unit sphere. The Lagrange multiplier equation at a maximizing vector v gives αv=λv, so α has a real unit eigenvector. Its orthogonal complement is invariant because
⟨αw,v⟩=⟨w,αv⟩=λ⟨w,v⟩=0.
(44)
Induction on the dimension supplies an orthonormal eigenbasis of that complement and hence of V.
For f=0,
⟨f,f⟩=∫0∞​f(x)2e−xdx>0,
(45)
while symmetry and bilinearity are immediate, so the displayed formula defines an inner product on Pn​. Since
e−xα(f)=(xe−xf′(x))′,
(46)
integration by parts gives
⟨αf,g⟩​=[gxe−xf′]0∞​−∫0∞​xe−xf′g′dx=⟨f,αg⟩.​
(47)
The boundary term vanishes for polynomials, proving that α is self-adjoint.
On the monomial xk,
α(xk)=−kxk+k2xk−1.
(48)
Thus the matrix of α in the monomial basis is triangular with diagonal
0,−1,−2,…,−n.
(49)

1,x−1,x2−4x+2​
(50)
for eigenvalues 0,−1,−2, respectively. They are the first Laguerre polynomials up to normalization, as described by the Laguerre differential operator on polynomials.

A polynomial over a unique factorization domain is primitive when the greatest common divisor of its coefficients is a unit.
Assume that the primitive polynomial f factors in F[X] as f=gh, with both factors of positive degree. Clearing denominators and removing contents writes
g=ag0​,h=bh0​,
(51)
where a,b∈F× and g0​,h0​∈R[X] are primitive. Then
f=abg0​h0​.
(52)
By Gauss lemma for polynomials, g0​h0​ is primitive. Since f is also primitive, comparison of contents forces ab to be a unit of R. Absorbing that unit into one factor gives a nontrivial factorization of f in R[X], contrary to its assumed irreducibility. Hence f is irreducible in F[X].

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
To deduce the final assertion, use the characterization that an integral domain is a unique factorization domain when it is atomic and every irreducible element is prime. Factoring the contents in R and then the primitive parts by degree shows that R[X] is atomic.
An irreducible constant of R is prime in R[X]. Every irreducible polynomial of positive degree is, up to a constant unit, primitive. Part (i) makes it irreducible in F[X]; because F[X] is a principal ideal domain, it is prime there, and part (ii) makes it prime in R[X]. Thus every irreducible of R[X] is prime, and
R[X] is a unique factorization domain.​
(54)
This is the polynomial ring over a unique factorization domain theorem.

For a∈U, the function f:U→Rn is differentiable at a if there is a linear map A:Rm→Rn such that
f(a+h)=f(a)+Ah+r(h),∥h∥∥r(h)∥​⟶0as h⟶0.
(58)
The linear map is unique and is the Frechet derivative Dfa​=A. The function is continuously differentiable at a if it is differentiable on a neighbourhood of a and the map x↦Dfx​, with values in the space of linear maps equipped with the operator norm, is continuous at a.
If T:Rm→Rn is linear, then
T(a+h)−T(a)−T(h)=0.
(59)
Consequently DTa​=T at every a. The derivative is a constant function of a, hence is continuous, so every linear map is continuously differentiable everywhere.
The mean value inequality says that if the line segment [x,y] lies in U and
∥Dfz​∥≤M(z∈[x,y]),
(60)
then
∥f(y)−f(x)∥≤M∥y−x∥.
(61)
To prove it, put v=f(y)−f(x). The claim is immediate if v=0. Otherwise set e=v/∥v∥ and apply the one-dimensional mean value theorem to the real-valued function
ϕ(t)=e⋅f(x+t(y−x)),0≤t≤1.
(62)
For some c∈(0,1), the chain rule gives
∥f(y)−f(x)∥​=ϕ(1)−ϕ(0)=e⋅Dfx+c(y−x)​(y−x)≤∥Dfx+c(y−x)​∥∥y−x∥≤M∥y−x∥,​
(63)
as required.
Now suppose that U is open and connected and that Dfa​=0 for every a∈U. Every point has an open ball contained in U. The mean value inequality with M=0 shows that f is constant on each such ball, so f is locally constant. Fix a0​∈U. The level set
E={x∈U:f(x)=f(a0​)}
(64)
is nonempty and open in U; its complement is also open because f is locally constant. Since U is connected, E=U. This proves the zero derivative on a connected open set result: f is constant.
The inverse function theorem states that if f:U→Rm is continuously differentiable, a∈U, and Dfa​ is an invertible linear map, then there are open neighbourhoods V of a and W of f(a) such that f∣V​:V→W is a bijection whose inverse is continuously differentiable.
For the curve in the question, define the continuously differentiable function
F(x,y)=x2+y+cos(xy)−1.
(65)
Then
F(0,0)=0,∂y∂F​(x,y)=1−xsin(xy),∂y∂F​(0,0)=1=0.
(66)
The implicit function theorem, which follows from the inverse function theorem applied to (x,y)↦(x,F(x,y)), therefore gives an open interval I containing 0, an open neighbourhood U0​ of (0,0), and a continuously differentiable, hence continuous, function g:I→R such that
U0​∩C={(x,y)∈R2:x∈I, y=g(x)}.

Rouché's theorem states that if g and h are holomorphic functions on a neighbourhood of the closure of a bounded domain and
∣h(z)∣<∣g(z)∣
(88)
on its positively oriented boundary, then g and g+h have the same number of zeros in the domain, counted with multiplicity.
The Open mapping theorem states that a nonconstant holomorphic function on a domain maps every open subset to an open subset. To prove it, fix z0​ and put w0​=f(z0​). By the identity theorem, the zeros of f−w0​ are isolated. Choose r>0 so that the closed disc D(z0​,r)​ lies in the domain and z0​ is the only zero of f−w0​ in that disc. Then
δ=min∣z−z0​∣=r​∣f(z)−w0​∣>0.
(89)
Whenever ∣w−w0​∣<δ, the constant w0​−w has modulus smaller than f−w0​ on the circle. The Rouche theorem therefore says that
f(z)−w=(f(z)−w0​)+(w0​−w)
(90)
has the same positive number of zeros in the disc as f−w0​. Thus every w∈D(w0​,δ) lies in the image of f, proving that the image is open.
If ∣f∣ had a local maximum at z0​, take a small open disc D on which ∣f(z)∣≤∣f(z0​)∣. The restriction of f to D cannot be constant, since the identity theorem would then make f constant on the whole domain. The complex open mapping theorem says that f(D) is an open neighbourhood of f(z0​), and such a neighbourhood contains points of modulus greater than ∣f(z0​)∣, a contradiction. This proves the maximum modulus principle from the complex open mapping theorem.
Now let Ω be bounded. Its closure is compact, so the continuous function ∣f∣ attains a maximum there. If f is nonconstant, the maximum modulus principle excludes an interior maximum; if f is constant, the claimed bound is immediate. Hence
maxz∈Ω​∣f(z)∣=maxz∈∂Ω​∣f(z)∣≤M,
(91)
which is the maximum modulus principle on a bounded domain.
Finally let Ω={z:Rez>1} and suppose ∣f∣≤K throughout Ω. Fix z0​∈Ω. The principal complex logarithm is holomorphic on the right half-plane, so for each positive integer n the function
gn​(z)=f(z)z−1/n=f(z)exp(−n1​Logz)
(92)
is holomorphic on Ω and continuous on its closure. Given ε>0, choose R>∣z0​∣ so large that
KR−1/n≤M+ε.
(93)
Apply the bounded-domain result to gn​ on Ω∩D(0,R). On the vertical part of the boundary, ∣z∣≥1 and hence ∣gn​(z)∣≤M. On the circular part,
∣gn​(z)∣≤KR−1/n≤M+ε.
(94)
It follows that
∣f(z0​)∣≤(M+ε)∣z0​∣1/n.
(95)
Letting n→∞ and then ε→0 gives ∣f(z0​)∣≤M. Since z0​ was arbitrary, this proves the bounded half-plane maximum principle.
The boundedness assumption is necessary. The function
f(z)=ez
(96)
is holomorphic on Ω and continuous on its closure, and ∣f(1+iy)∣=e on the boundary, but ∣f(x)∣=ex is unbounded for real x>1. Thus the boundary estimate does not control an unbounded holomorphic function on this unbounded domain.

A possibly randomized test is a function φ(X)∈[0,1], interpreted as the conditional probability of rejecting H0​. Its power function is
πφ​(θ)=Eθ​[φ(X)].
(151)
It has size at most α when
supθ∈Θ0​​πφ​(θ)≤α.
(152)
Such a test is a uniformly most powerful test of size α if, for every other test ψ of size at most α,
πφ​(θ)≥πψ​(θ)for every θ∈Θ1​.
(153)
Thus one test maximizes power simultaneously at every parameter value in the alternative.
